papers.title: The opposing informational effects of AI trading
papers.abstract: Better artificial intelligence (AI) can improve individual forecasts without making prices better at revealing new information. In a competitive market with resource-constrained forecasting, more capable algorithms can substitute analysis of public records for private observations, reducing the private information aggregated into prices. The same trades can convey sophisticated public-data analysis to investors unable to perform it themselves. We establish conditions under which these effects coexist and the private benefit of further computation falls. Numerical equilibrium calculations and finite-data neural-market experiments exhibit corresponding patterns. Out-of-sample earnings forecasts and controlled language-model tasks show related patterns of information substitution. In the neural experiment, wider adoption increases the predictive value of price for limited observers, reduces it for advanced observers, and lowers the benefit of upgrading by 44\%. Retraining by investors who did not upgrade can amplify the loss of private-information precision. The informational consequences of AI trading depend on what prices reveal and who can use them.

papers.title: JaxMARL-BC: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Macroeconomic Modelling, in Seconds
papers.abstract: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) offers a principled way of populating simulated economies with many heterogeneous decision makers. Its adoption, pioneered in finance, has nonetheless been slow in macroeconomics because of two main limitations: the lack of a shared frame of reference connecting MARL systems to dynamic stochastic general equilibrium (DSGE) models the profession already trusts, and the very long training times. The first limitation was recently addressed by the Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Business Cycle (MARL-BC), which places deep RL households in a real business cycle economy and reduces to classic DSGE models in specific limits. Here we address the second limitation. We present JaxMARL-BC, a JAX-accelerated simulator that trains MARL-BC economies in seconds (between 75x and 724x faster than the reference implementation), and scales to 200,000 independent learning households. We verify its correctness against the known DSGE limits, characterise its scaling through a simple cost law, and demonstrate its value by a proof-of-concept calibration of an extended model with heterogeneous returns on capital, in a two-hour experiment that would previously have taken over a month. We release JaxMARL-BC as open source.

papers.title: Revisiting the ABCs of Working with AI: Evidence from Radiologists
papers.abstract: I examine the relationship between the benefits of working with AI and two baseline traits - ability and belief calibration - among all 227 radiologists available in Collab-CXR, a dataset from an experiment where AI assistance was provided during X-ray diagnosis. When analyzed jointly, both lower unassisted accuracy and smaller miscalibration, measured by the absolute gap between average confidence and accuracy, are associated with greater improvements in accuracy with AI. In addition, the association between unassisted accuracy and improvement with AI becomes more negative and statistically significant when controlling for calibration.

papers.title: How optimistic inflow forecasts distort dispatch, prices, and contracts in hydro-dominated power systems: evidence from Brazil
papers.abstract: Centralized hydrothermal planning models determine generation schedules and electricity spot prices based on inflow forecasts in audited-cost power systems, such as those prevalent in Latin America, and provide operational benchmarks and decision support in hydro-dominated competitive electricity markets. Consequently, biased forecasts can propagate directly into both operational decisions and market outcomes. This paper studies how persistent optimistic inflow forecast bias can propagate through a hydrothermal power system, from system operation to market outcomes. For a stylized hydrothermal model, we show that optimistic bias weakly reduces water values and weakly increases first-stage hydro discharge relative to the unbiased optimum, thereby lowering reservoir storage and postponing thermal commitment. Using official Brazilian planning and operational data, we provide empirical evidence consistent with this mechanism. We then conduct controlled SDDP experiments to compare policies trained under biased and bias-corrected inflow-forecast processes, evaluating both under the same bias-corrected inflow scenarios. The policy based on biased forecasts produces lower reservoir levels, delayed dry-season thermal dispatch, sharper spot-price peaks, higher reliability risk, and higher expected operating costs. Finally, a stylized contracting exercise indicates that these distortions increase the price-quantity risk of a representative hydropower producer and reduce its willingness-to-contract. The results indicate that inflow-forecast bias can be a source of operational inefficiency, reliability risk, and distorted market incentives in hydro-dominated power systems. The insights and policy implications drawn in this paper may be relevant to hydro-dominated systems and electricity markets that are increasingly reliant on energy storage.

papers.title: Economic Power in International Trade
papers.abstract: Economic power is a country's capacity to harm another more than itself by withdrawing from a trading relationship. This paper develops a general equilibrium model of the world trade network to measure that power through counterfactual sanctions. Using a world input-output table of eighty economies and fifty industries, we solve for $3{,}160$ such sanction equilibria, one for each bilateral severance of a trading relationship. We read the asymmetry between the two sides' losses as power. Our results show that mutual trade dependence is anything but mutual. The distribution of power in world trade is highly skewed. In the median trade relationship, one country inflicts on its trading partner more than four times the loss it bears. Only one pair in seven is close to balanced. The United States is more powerful than all seventy-nine of its partners and China against all but one. Economic power is not determined by the bilateral trade balance.

papers.title: China's Local Government Debt, Strategic Competition, and Bitcoin Demand: A Conditional Transmission Framework
papers.abstract: How might the resolution of China's local-government debt affect strategic competition and Bitcoin demand? This paper develops a conditional framework connecting debt accounting, bank balance-sheet adjustment, public spending priorities, and constrained portfolio substitution. A debt swap can increase recognized government debt without increasing consolidated principal, while its effect on credit capacity depends on capital relief, loss recognition, and recapitalization. A protected strategic-spending floor can preserve current effort while shifting adjustment toward civilian productive services. In the asset block, stronger relative preference for Bitcoin does not ensure greater effective demand: access constraints and global funding conditions can reverse the sign. We derive a finite-shock threshold and deterministic sign bounds, and distinguish Bitcoin demand from demand for dollar stablecoins. Reproducible numerical illustrations and channel-removal exercises show that opposite outcomes are compatible with the same assumed fiscal stress. The analysis uses dated primary sources to establish institutional context, but estimates neither a debt-to-Bitcoin causal coefficient nor a price-impact scale. Its contribution is a compact set of conditions and measurement distinctions for evaluating transmission claims, rather than an unconditional price forecast or an inference about conflict probabilities.

papers.title: Corporate Stances on Societal Issues in the US
papers.abstract: When do firms take public positions on divisive societal issues and why? We assemble a comprehensive dataset on corporate stance-taking in the United States, using large language models to read 52,000 news articles and press releases about 836 companies that belonged to the S&P 500 at any point between 2008 and 2025. We identify 9,917 stances on nine partisan issues such as climate change, abortion, and racial discrimination. We show that stance-taking increased fourfold after 2008 and peaked in 2021. It is overwhelmingly liberal and concentrated among the largest firms. A quarter of stances give no explicit business justification. Stance-taking is only weakly related to lobbying and campaign contributions and, unlike them, does not follow the electoral cycle. Instead, firms tend to speak when media coverage and public interest in an issue peak. Together, these findings suggest that stance-taking can be understood as a contribution to broad policy debates rather than a strategy to shape policies that affect firms' core business. Finally, we investigate whose views corporate stances represent. Consumer-facing firms take more stances, and firms whose consumers lean Democratic take more liberal stances on issues other than climate. Companies with larger shares of Democratic employees, executives, and board members also take more liberal stances. Exploiting within-firm variation, we find that having more Democrats among a company's leadership increases liberal stance-taking, while having more women increases stance-taking on gender-related issues and abortion.

papers.title: Identifying Time Preference Shocks: Stated and Revealed Preferences after an Italian Earthquake
papers.abstract: Identifying time preference shocks is challenging: shocks large enough to shift survey-elicited stated impatience also tighten financial resources, confounding the interpretation of stated time preference. Jointly examining stated and revealed preferences resolves this identification problem: impatience shocks and reductions in financial resources generate opposite consumption responses, even though both raise stated impatience. Applying our identification framework to the 2009 L'Aquila earthquake, we combine panel data with spatially granular seismic and damage data in a difference-in-differences design that compares undamaged households that experienced the earthquake with a spatial control group at similar distances from the epicenter. Treated households report greater impatience and increase nondurable consumption by 11 percent relative to controls. Effects are consistent with a psychological stress channel, concentrated among the most vulnerable to stress, and persist as households deplete their liquid wealth buffer over time.

papers.title: Trade Tensions Meet the Gig Economy: Evidence from the 2025 Halving of Chinese Travel to Japan
papers.abstract: How do geopolitical shocks to services exports reach local labor markets? Using China's November 2025 Japan travel advisory and postings on Japan's largest spot-work platform, we provide the first such evidence for the gig economy. Posted hourly wages fall immediately and persistently in prefectures more dependent on Chinese visitors, relative to others, whereas postings, hours, and employment show no robust change. Wages fall more for early morning and daytime shifts, when hotels and shops hire, than for evening and night shifts. Where each shift is priced anew, a services-trade shock lowers the price of labor in the hours it hits.

papers.title: A Game of Throngs: How Spotlight Tourism Reshapes Local Economies
papers.abstract: In July 2017, San Juan de Gaztelugatxe, a modest chapel in the Basque Country, appeared as "Dragonstone" in Game of Thrones, transforming a locally known site with limited tourism activity into a global tourist destination overnight. We exploit this exogenous spotlight shock to estimate its causal effects on the local economy using a novel administrative dataset and a Synthetic Control approach. We find an abrupt increase in tourism activity, far exceeding the effects documented in the literature. Despite this surge, employment gains in tourism-related sectors were largely offset by losses elsewhere, resulting in no net effect on total employment. We also document signs of housing-market overheating, with increases in both property transactions and prices. We find no evidence that the shock displaced the local population. Instead, it led to a roughly twofold increase in arrivals from abroad. Taken together, these findings suggest that a substantial increase in tourism activity does not necessarily translate into broad-based local economic gains. Instead, tourism-led growth may entail significant sectoral reallocation and housing-market pressures, underscoring the importance of looking beyond tourism activity alone when assessing its wider economic effects.

papers.title: The Geoengineering Put: Ecological Debt, Termination Risk, and Asset Prices
papers.abstract: Solar geoengineering offers an inexpensive and fast-acting way to lower global temperatures without removing carbon from the atmosphere. As warming intensifies, climate-vulnerable countries face growing incentives to deploy geoengineering unilaterally. The economic and financial consequences of this prospect remain largely overlooked. We develop a general equilibrium macro-finance framework in which geoengineering acts as a put option on climate damages, funded by the "ecological debt" of masked warming. If deployment stops, temperatures snap back in a catastrophic termination shock. Anticipation of geoengineering raises current brown firm valuations and lowers the optimal carbon tax, helping explain two puzzles in the existing literature: high brown-firm valuations and low carbon taxes. As ecological debt grows, however, termination risk transforms brown firms into toxic assets. Geoengineering also reshapes green innovation: it buys time for a breakthrough, but can weaken innovation incentives by lowering energy and carbon prices. Termination risk partly restores research incentives and directs them toward carbon removal, which can retire ecological debt. Our calibrations show that the geoengineering put can raise welfare across a range of parameter assumptions. Our framework clarifies how this conclusion depends on uncertain parameters and where further research is most needed.

papers.title: The Narrow Corridor of Stable Solutions in an Extended Osipov--Lanchester Model with Constant Total Population
papers.abstract: This paper studies a modification of the classical Osipov-Lanchester model in which the total population of the two sides, $N=R+B$, stays constant. In this model the ratio $y=R/B$ obeys the Riccati equation $\dot y=\alpha y^2-\beta$, which is solvable in elementary functions for all values of the parameters. The main result is a complete classification of the stable regimes. An asymptotically stable invariant set in the quadrant $R,B\ge 0$ exists only in three cases: $\alpha<0,\ \beta<0$ gives a stable interior equilibrium; $\alpha=0,\ \beta<0$ makes the boundary $B=0$ stable; $\alpha<0,\ \beta=0$ makes the boundary $R=0$ stable. If $\alpha>0$ or $\beta>0$, every solution except one unstable equilibrium reaches a boundary of the quadrant in finite time, where the model stops being applicable. If the parameters vary in time, a fixed distance from the boundaries is kept when $\alpha(t)$ and $\beta(t)$ obey buffer dynamics that push them away from zero. Finally, in the case $\alpha<0,\ \beta<0$ the original system grows exponentially, while in the two degenerate cases it grows at most linearly. Growth demanded of a given cost, the sum of the two channels, bounds their imbalance and, with the perturbation bound, confines the parameters to an explicit wedge about $|\alpha|=|\beta|$ truncated near the origin: the narrow corridor of the model.

papers.title: The Anatomy of Value Creation: Input-Output Linkages, Policy Shifts, and Economic Impacts
papers.abstract: This paper describes the construction of high-resolution 7-digit product-level Supply-Use Tables (SUTs) and symmetric Input-Output Tables (IOTs) for the Indian economy from 2016-17 to 2022-23, primarily utilising microdata from the Annual Survey of Industries (ASI). It outlines the intricate methodology for generating comprehensive input and output flows, reconciling data from registered and unregistered manufacturing sectors using NPCMS-NIC concordance, and transforming SUTs into analytically robust IOTs via the Industry Technology Assumption. The paper demonstrates the application of this framework through an in-depth case study of India's mobile phone manufacturing sector (NPCMS 4722200), analysing its economic impact, particularly on Domestic Value Added (DVA) and employment. The findings reveal significant structural shifts, including output growth, import substitution, export surges, and evolving labour dynamics. These detailed tables represent a valuable advancement for analysing sectoral interdependencies, the efficacy of industrial policy, and enhancing India's National Accounts Statistics, resonating with the NSS's legacy of data-driven policymaking.

papers.title: When AI Improves Answers but Slows Knowledge Creation: Matching and Dynamic Knowledge Creation in Digital Public Goods
papers.abstract: Generative AI helps users solve problems more efficiently, but can also replace exchanges between people with private conversations with chatbots. When more problems are solved privately, fewer problem-solving episodes are converted into reusable public knowledge for others. We build a dynamic model of public good provision where agents post and answer questions on a public platform. AI can shrink the platform's archive through two margins. Private diversion can reduce the posted volume of knowledge-enhancing questions (the flow margin), while contributor exit can lower conditional resolution (the resolution margin). Low-archive traps can arise with or without AI, because a thin archive makes public answering too costly to sustain; AI can narrow the viable region. The model gives conditional empirical predictions that distinguish demand-side diversion from supply-side pool thinning under explicit identifying restrictions. Logging private solutions adds archive inflow, while rewards for answering strengthen contribution incentives.

papers.title: How an Economy Shrinks in Space: Concavity-on-Jobs and Upward Consolidation under Demographic Decline
papers.abstract: When a country's population declines, the aggregate economy appears to contract on the intensive margin: industrial diversity intact, every industry a little smaller. At the regional level, contraction is uneven and takes the extensive form: entire industries disappear, one after another. The relevant unit is the city: industries are nested by size - the hierarchy property of industrial location - each viable only above a minimum population. Necessity industries' thresholds bunch at the low end, so a city's industry count - and its jobs - is sharply concave in size (concavity on jobs). A modest loss pushes a small city below many thresholds at once; a large core sheds a few specialized industries, one at a time. Lost industries consolidate upward to the next city large enough to host them; for the worker it means a step down to a lower-paid local job if one is left, and a fall to the bottom of the hierarchy if none is. To recover the lost wage, workers move up to the apex - the only city hosting the full industry range. In Japan - two decades ahead of the OECD, Tokyo at its apex - a wage regression in real, housing-inclusive wages, on worker-level panel data for the young workers who carry the migration, finds a Tokyo-bound migration incentive that varies across origins exactly as concavity on jobs predicts.

papers.title: Complements or Substitutes? Technology Adoption and Clinical Care Utilization: Evidence from Automated Insulin Delivery
papers.abstract: Whether medical technology reduces or increases demand for professional care is central to understanding its effects on healthcare utilization and costs. We study automated insulin delivery (AID) adoption among 1,608 adults with type 1 diabetes treated in four specialist clinics of the Italian National Health Service, 283 of whom adopt AID. Because adoption is clinically targeted and staggered, we combine risk-set coarsened exact matching with a staggered event-study design. Matching retains 181 adopters with comparable untreated controls. We further adjust for differential pre-adoption trends by extrapolating the untreated trajectory in event time. After adjustment, AID adoption is associated with greater routine outpatient engagement. The estimated effect on the probability of a diabetologist visit is 16.3 percentage points one semester after adoption and 39.3 percentage points four semesters after adoption, relative to a 55.2% visit probability in the semester before adoption. HbA1c testing and a broader process-of-care index show similar positive patterns, although the evidence is less precise. The visit estimates remain sensitive to the trend-extrapolation assumption and should therefore be interpreted conditionally on that restriction. The findings are consistent with a task-based view in which automation substitutes for routine dosing decisions while complementing clinical labor through interpretive, adjustment, and supervisory tasks. Patient-facing automation may therefore reorganize rather than simply reduce healthcare use.

papers.title: That Time of the Year Again: Government Pay Revisions in the Aggregate Economy
papers.abstract: Public pay is set by law in nominal terms, so inflation erodes its real value between legal acts until the government revises it. I model each revision as the choice of a forward-looking government, shaped by two costs that push in opposite directions. A fixed cost of acting makes revisions large and rare, whereas a convex cost of financing the increase at once makes them small and frequent. Through the budget, each revision also moves debt and the risk of fiscal stress under which the next one is made. In the documented pay decisions of eleven countries, pay set at discretion erodes against prices and private earnings and is restored in discrete steps, every cut was decided during market stress or an adjustment program, and court rulings drove a wedge between the cuts legislated, the cuts paid and the cuts that lasted. Estimated on the legal acts, the model reproduces the documented paths of pay in most countries when data and simulations are measured the same way. In Portugal's estimated model, the savings that the Treasury requires once spreads rise produce the cuts, the debt overhang holds pay down after the crisis, and a court that strikes cuts after they take effect invites cuts it will strike. Review of cuts before they took effect would have lowered the social cost of Portugal's crisis relative to review after the fact, and partial indexation would have paid in Bangladesh unless its automatic increases were costly to finance.
